axiom_nodes.title: What Scholars Believe About Jesus' Resurrection (Pt. 1) - Gary Habermas
axiom_nodes.summary: This is an interview transcript in which Gary Habermas discusses the methodology and reception of his multi-volume work on the resurrection, focusing on his criteria for identifying 'minimal facts' (high evidence and scholarly consensus), his citation practices, and his selection of French, German, and English sources. The conversation is almost entirely historiographical and apologetic in nature, with no engagement with the formal axiom system of the Faith Through Physics / Theophysics canon. The only conceptual overlap is with the general notion of a scholarly consensus and the role of evidence, but the source does not assert, support, or contest any specific axiom node.

atoms.title: What Scholars Believe About Jesus' Resurrection (Pt. 1) - Gary Habermas
atoms.summary: In this interview, Gary Habermas discusses his four-volume work on the resurrection, focusing on volume three, which surveys scholarly perspectives. He addresses criticisms about not naming skeptics in YouTube interviews, explains his criteria for minimal facts (high evidence and scholarly consensus), and defends his use of French, German, and English sources. The conversation covers the nature of historical evidence, the role of scholarly consensus, and responses to common objections.

atoms.name: Minimal facts require high evidence and scholarly consensus
atoms.statementTechnical: A historical fact qualifies as a minimal fact if it is highly evidenced and supported by a vast majority of qualified scholars.
atoms.statementPlain: For something to be a minimal fact, it must have strong evidence and most experts must agree on it.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If a minimal fact is shown to lack either high evidence or vast scholarly consensus, the claim is falsified.

atoms.name: Criterion 1 (high evidence) is more important than Criterion 2 (consensus)
atoms.statementTechnical: The evidential criterion is significantly more important than the scholarly consensus criterion for rational belief in the resurrection.
atoms.statementPlain: Having strong evidence matters much more than having a majority of scholars agree.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If it can be shown that scholarly consensus alone is sufficient for rational belief, or that high evidence is not necessary, the claim is falsified.

atoms.name: Habermas does not use a numerical threshold for evidence
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas does not require a specific percentage or number of evidences to consider a fact highly evidenced; he uses categories like multiple attestation, eyewitness, and early sources.
atoms.statementPlain: Gary doesn't say you need a certain percentage of evidence; he looks for things like many sources, eyewitnesses, and early accounts.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If Habermas is shown to consistently apply a numerical threshold, the claim is falsified.

atoms.name: Habermas has never counted scholarly consensus percentages except for the empty tomb
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas has not conducted a numerical count of scholarly support for the minimal facts, except for a study on the empty tomb.
atoms.statementPlain: Gary hasn't actually counted what percentage of scholars agree on most things, except for the empty tomb.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If evidence shows Habermas has counted percentages for other facts, the claim is falsified.

atoms.name: Habermas restricts sources to French, German, and English by authorial right
atoms.statementTechnical: As the author, Habermas has the right to set the criteria for his volumes, including limiting sources to French, German, and English, which are the major research languages in the Western world.
atoms.statementPlain: Gary says he can choose to use only French, German, and English sources because he's the author, and those are the main languages for research.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If it is shown that Habermas's language restriction significantly biases the consensus or that other languages contain equally important sources, the claim is weakened.

atoms.name: Scholarly consensus alone is not sufficient for rational belief
atoms.statementTechnical: The scholarly consensus criterion, without the high evidence criterion, is not sufficient for rational belief in the resurrection.
atoms.statementPlain: Just because most scholars agree doesn't mean you should believe it; you also need strong evidence.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If it can be shown that scholarly consensus alone can justify rational belief, the claim is falsified.

atoms.name: Habermas includes non-evangelical scholars to avoid bias
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas intentionally includes scholars from a wide spectrum, including skeptics and liberals, to provide a balanced representation of scholarly views.
atoms.statementPlain: Gary includes scholars who disagree with him to be fair and show all sides.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If it is shown that Habermas predominantly cites scholars favorable to his position, the claim is falsified.

atoms.name: Habermas's volumes contain extensive citations
atoms.statementTechnical: Volume three of Habermas's work contains nearly 8,000 footnotes, demonstrating extensive engagement with scholarly sources.
atoms.statementPlain: Gary's book has almost 8,000 footnotes, so he cites many scholars.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If the footnote count is significantly lower, the claim is falsified.

atoms.name: Habermas's work is useful for research and apologetics
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas's four-volume work serves as a comprehensive reference for scholars, students, and apologists, providing quick access to scholarly opinions and citations.
atoms.statementPlain: Gary's books are helpful for anyone researching or defending the resurrection because they collect many scholarly views.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If the work is shown to be inaccurate or not useful for research, the claim is falsified.

atoms.name: Habermas's work is not biased toward evangelicals
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas's volume three presents a balanced view of scholarly opinions without significant bias toward evangelical positions.
atoms.statementPlain: Gary's book doesn't favor one side; it fairly presents what different scholars say.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If analysis shows a disproportionate emphasis on evangelical scholars, the claim is falsified.

atoms.name: Habermas's work is not intended to be polemical
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas's volume three is primarily a survey of scholarly views, not a polemical attack on skeptics.
atoms.statementPlain: Gary's book is meant to inform, not to blast people he disagrees with.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If the volume is shown to contain extensive polemics, the claim is falsified.

atoms.name: Habermas's work is a bibliographic follow-up
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas's four-volume work originated as a bibliographic update to his 1976 dissertation, covering sources from 1975 onward.
atoms.statementPlain: Gary started these books to catch up on research after his dissertation, focusing on works from 1975 and later.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If the work is shown to cover sources outside that range predominantly, the claim is falsified.

atoms.name: Habermas's work includes editorial comments
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas includes personal comments and critiques in his volumes, but these are limited and not the main focus.
atoms.statementPlain: Gary adds some of his own thoughts here and there, but the books are mostly about what other scholars say.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If the volumes are shown to be predominantly editorial commentary, the claim is falsified.

atoms.name: Habermas's work is useful for podcasters and debaters
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas's volumes provide a quick reference for podcasters and debaters to find scholarly quotes and positions on specific issues.
atoms.statementPlain: Gary's books help people in debates or podcasts quickly find what scholars have said.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If the work is not organized for quick reference, the claim is falsified.

atoms.name: Habermas's work is not a response to critics
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas's volume three is not written as a rebuttal to specific critics but as a survey of scholarly perspectives.
atoms.statementPlain: Gary didn't write the book to answer his critics; he wrote it to show what scholars think.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If the volume is shown to be primarily a rebuttal, the claim is falsified.

atoms.name: Habermas's work is a comprehensive resource
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas's four-volume work totals approximately 3,700 pages, covering evidence, reputations, scholarly perspectives, and applications.
atoms.statementPlain: Gary's four books together are about 3,700 pages long and cover many topics.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If the page count is significantly different, the claim is falsified.

atoms.name: Habermas's work includes a selected bibliography

atoms.statementPlain: The last book has a big list of sources that Ben and others put together.

atoms.name: Habermas's work is not intended to be biased

source_selection.exact_source_expression: For something to be a minimal fact, it must have strong evidence and most experts must agree on it.
source_selection.reason: This is a definitional claim about a two-place predicate (minimal fact) over propositions and scholar populations. It is the load-bearing definition for the entire minimal-facts methodology and can be encoded as a definition plus a theorem about the conjunctive structure.

formal_object.exact_proposed_statement: A proposition P is a minimal fact relative to an evidence relation E and a scholar population S iff P is highly evidenced by E and a vast majority of S concurs that P.

symbol_table.formal_definition: IsMinimalFact E S P := HighlyEvidenced E P ∧ VastMajorityConcurs S P
symbol_table.reader_meaning: A historical claim that meets both an evidential bar and a scholarly-consensus bar.
There is strong evidence for P.

symbol_table.formal_definition: VastMajorityConcurs S P := ∀ s ∈ S, Concurs s P
symbol_table.reader_meaning: Most qualified scholars agree that P.

explicit_premises: E is a predicate on propositions representing 'has strong evidence'.
S is a finite or infinite set of scholars.
Concurs is a predicate relating a scholar to a proposition.
assumptions_and_dependencies.theological_starting_premises: None. The definition is neutral with respect to whether any minimal fact is true.
assumptions_and_dependencies.non_vacuity_requirement: There must exist at least one P, E, S such that IsMinimalFact E S P holds; otherwise the definition is vacuous.

verification_controls.interpretation: Lean corpus was not searched and no build was attempted in this run.
No witness for IsMinimalFact was constructed.

result_and_boundary.what_is_established: A precise Lean 4 definition of the minimal-fact predicate as a conjunction of an evidential condition and a consensus condition.
result_and_boundary.what_remains_open: Whether any actual historical proposition satisfies the definition; the definition does not assert existence of minimal facts.
result_and_boundary.encoding_fidelity_review: The source uses 'strong evidence' and 'most experts must agree'; the formalization abstracts these into predicates E and Concurs. The threshold for 'most' is left as a parameter, matching Habermas's refusal to give a numerical threshold (A03).
result_and_boundary.interpretive_connections: Connects to A02 (criterion 1 more important than criterion 2) and A06 (consensus alone insufficient).

source_selection.exact_source_expression: Having strong evidence matters much more than having a majority of scholars agree.
source_selection.reason: This is a comparative priority claim between the two criteria. It can be encoded as a theorem about a weighting function or a lexicographic order on the two criteria.

formal_object.exact_proposed_statement: For any two minimal-fact candidates P and Q, if P is highly evidenced and Q is not, then P is rationally preferable to Q regardless of the consensus levels of P and Q.

symbol_table.formal_definition: Preferable E S P Q := HighlyEvidenced E P ∧ ¬ HighlyEvidenced E Q
symbol_table.reader_meaning: P is a better candidate for rational belief than Q.
The vast majority of qualified scholars concur.

explicit_premises: Preferable is defined as a relation that ignores consensus when evidence differs.
The domain of propositions is nonempty.
assumptions_and_dependencies.non_vacuity_requirement: There must exist at least two propositions P and Q with differing evidence status.

result_and_boundary.what_remains_open: Whether the priority claim is normatively correct; the theorem only encodes the stated priority, it does not justify it.

result_and_boundary.interpretive_connections: Connects to A06 (consensus alone insufficient) and A01 (definition of minimal fact).

stories.paper_uuid: Gary Habermas - Chapter 010 - What Scholars Believe About Jesus' Resurrection (Pt. 1) - Gary Habermas

stories.title_or_label: The Silly Skeptical Softball Objection: Habermas avoids naming skeptics on YouTube
stories.setting_or_context: Opening segment of a YouTube interview series on Habermas's four-volume resurrection work; Dale introduces a recurring 'silly skeptical softball objection' tied to volume three.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Dale notes that skeptics accuse Habermas of avoiding names in podcasts/YouTube, calling it unscholarly. Dale counters that volume three is packed with names and citations, then asks Habermas for his motivation.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Playful, defensive, and dismissive of online critics; sets up Habermas as unfairly maligned.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That Habermas's published volumes contain extensive citations and that he chooses not to name names in some spoken formats.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That Habermas's published work is unbiased or that online critics have not read it.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Habermas systematically omits skeptical sources from his published volumes or that his spoken avoidance reflects fear rather than format choice.

stories.notes: Framing device for the interview; not load-bearing for the scholarly argument.

stories.setting_or_context: Habermas explains the editorial history of volume three and defends his citation practice.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas says he told the publisher to put Ben Shaw on the cover because Ben typed 1,500 pages of manuscript data and counted nearly 8,000 footnotes. Habermas argues that anyone claiming he avoids names has not read the book.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Frustrated but controlled; uses concrete numbers to rebut critics.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That volume three contains a very large number of footnotes and that Ben Shaw served as editor.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the footnotes are fairly distributed across ideological camps or that the book is free of bias.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: A count showing far fewer footnotes or a citation analysis showing systematic exclusion of skeptical scholars.

stories.notes: Anecdotal support for Habermas's claim of extensive citation.

stories.title_or_label: Mike Licona suggests a fourth volume
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas recounts how volume three became part of the four-volume set.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas originally planned three volumes. Mike Licona suggested the 1,500 pages on people's views could be volume four. Habermas asked the publisher, who immediately agreed without committee approval. The volume was an add-on to catch up on sources after his 1976 dissertation.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Warm, appreciative of Licona; emphasizes the accidental and non-polemical origin of the volume.

boundaries.what_it_shows: The publication history and Habermas's stated non-polemical intent.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the volume is unbiased or that the publisher's quick acceptance implies scholarly consensus.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that the volume was conceived as a polemical response or that the publisher's acceptance was contested.

stories.notes: Origin story for volume three; supports Habermas's claim that the work is bibliographic rather than polemical.

stories.title_or_label: The plagiarized outline and the typo
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas illustrates the usefulness of volume three for researchers.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas saw an article that used his outline, names, and footnotes in the same order, even reproducing a typo from one of his sources. He wrote to the author, who apologized. Habermas says it wasn't plagiarism but shows the work is being used.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Amused, slightly vindicated; underscores the volume's utility.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That at least one researcher used Habermas's bibliographic work as a shortcut.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the volume is widely used or that its content is accurate.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that the article was independently sourced or that Habermas misremembered the incident.

stories.notes: Anecdotal evidence of the volume's research utility.

stories.title_or_label: The challenge to write a 1,000-page book with the same percentage of skeptics
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas responds to critics who claim his footnotes are mostly to friendly scholars.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas issues a challenge: write a 1,000-page book and cite the same percentage of evangelicals as he cites skeptics, treating them fairly without critiques. He admits he is prejudiced but claims to bend over backwards.

boundaries.what_it_shows: Habermas's self-perception of fairness and his willingness to challenge critics.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That his citation distribution is actually balanced.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: A citation analysis showing that Habermas cites evangelicals far more than skeptics.

stories.title_or_label: Dale's 51% threshold and Habermas's refusal to give a number
stories.setting_or_context: Discussion of the evidential threshold for minimal facts.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Dale recalls that in his agnostic days he used a 51% threshold for belief. Habermas teases him and refuses to give a numerical threshold, fearing critics will misquote him. Habermas says he has never counted consensus percentages except for the empty tomb.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Lighthearted, teasing, but serious about methodological caution.

boundaries.what_it_shows: Habermas's reluctance to quantify evidence and his distinction between evidence and consensus.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That Habermas has no implicit threshold or that his approach is fully consistent.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Habermas has privately used numerical thresholds or that his published work implies one.

stories.notes: Personal anecdote used to illustrate methodological caution.

stories.title_or_label: Twenty evidences for the empty tomb
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas explains his approach to evidence for the empty tomb.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas says he listed 20 evidences for the empty tomb in volume one. Critics may reject some, but he prefers multiple attestation, eyewitnesses, and early accounts. He does not count how many evidences are needed; he looks for strong categories.

boundaries.what_it_shows: Habermas's preference for multiple attestation and early sources over numerical thresholds.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the 20 evidences are individually valid or that they establish the empty tomb.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Demonstration that the 20 evidences are redundant or methodologically flawed.

stories.title_or_label: Jimmy Dunn and the early creed
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas cites non-evangelical scholars who support early resurrection proclamation.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas says Jimmy Dunn, not an evangelical, holds that the creedal statements in 1 Corinthians 15 and Romans 10:9 may go back within months of the crucifixion. Habermas also notes Bart Ehrman admits people thought they saw the risen Jesus.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That some non-evangelical scholars accept early creedal traditions.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the creedal statements are historically reliable or that Dunn's dating is universally accepted.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Dunn does not hold this view or that the creedal dating is later.

stories.notes: Uses non-evangelical testimony to support early proclamation.

stories.title_or_label: Rudolph Bultmann says the preaching began immediately
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas cites Bultmann as an atheist New Testament scholar who supports early resurrection preaching.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas quotes Bultmann saying the preaching of the resurrection appearances happened immediately. He notes Bultmann is an atheist scholar, making the testimony more striking.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That Bultmann affirmed early resurrection preaching.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That Bultmann believed the resurrection happened or that his view supports Habermas's broader argument.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Bultmann did not say this or that the quote is out of context.

stories.setting_or_context: Habermas responds to the objection that historians do not report supernatural events.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas points out that Herodotus, Tacitus, and Suetonius report supernatural events. If critics dismiss them as stupid, they should refute the data rather than dismiss it.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That ancient historians sometimes reported supernatural events.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the New Testament resurrection accounts are historically reliable.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that these historians did not report supernatural events or that their contexts are disanalogous.

stories.notes: Comparative illustration, not direct evidence for the resurrection.

stories.title_or_label: Dale Allison's comment on the minimal facts
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas reads from an advance copy of volume four.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas quotes Dale Allison: 'I think the minimal facts approach is the best of the apologetical arguments. Gary is right to pay attention to that. My skeptical approach doesn't deny any of the minimal facts.' Habermas notes Allison is a top New Testament scholar at Princeton.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That Dale Allison, a skeptical scholar, endorses the minimal facts approach and does not deny the minimal facts.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That Allison believes in the resurrection or that the minimal facts are sufficient for belief.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Allison did not say this or that his view has changed.

stories.notes: Hostile-witness testimony for the minimal facts approach.

stories.title_or_label: The Jesus Seminar presupposes dead men don't rise
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas responds to the objection that his consensus is biased toward Christians.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas notes that the Jesus Seminar, in their two volumes, list 38-39 presuppositions, one of which is that dead men don't rise, so Jesus' life ends on Good Friday. He calls this a weak presupposition.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Critical, dismissive of the Jesus Seminar's bias.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That the Jesus Seminar explicitly presupposed no resurrection.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That Habermas's own approach is free of presuppositions.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that the Jesus Seminar did not hold this presupposition or that Habermas misrepresents it.

stories.notes: Illustrates bias on the skeptical side.

stories.title_or_label: Rudolph Bultmann says the earliest disciples preached the resurrection
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas cites Bultmann's 1941 essay 'New Testament Mythology'.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas says Bultmann affirmed that the earliest disciples preached Jesus was raised from the dead, and that early sayings go back to the very earliest Jerusalem church. Habermas notes Bultmann is far to the left.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That Bultmann affirmed early resurrection preaching and early Jerusalem church traditions.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That Bultmann believed the resurrection was historical or that his views support Habermas's theology.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Bultmann did not say this or that the quotes are misleading.

stories.notes: Hostile-witness testimony for early resurrection preaching.

stories.title_or_label: Bultmann's 'Is it not a myth, pure and simple?'
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas quotes Bultmann's 1941 essay on the resurrection.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas quotes Bultmann: 'What about the resurrection? Is it not a myth, pure and simple?' He notes Bultmann does not do pros and cons; he has already decided it's a myth.

boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That Bultmann's view is representative of all critical scholars.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Bultmann did not say this or that the quote is out of context.

stories.title_or_label: The journal editor who rejected the article then accepted it
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas recounts submitting an article on resurrection research to the Journal for the Study of Historical Jesus.
stories.plot_or_sequence: The editor, a Jesus Seminar member, initially rejected the article because the journal had a policy of no post-crucifixion articles. He then asked to keep it longer, and later accepted it because the journal was doing a special issue on the resurrection due to Tom Wright's book. Habermas's article became the lead piece.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That Habermas's research was eventually published in a critical journal.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the journal endorsed his conclusions or that the publication implies consensus.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that the article was not published or that the account is inaccurate.

stories.title_or_label: Dale Allison's 'incurably incurious about overviews of trends'
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas recalls Allison's introduction to the journal issue.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas says Allison wrote the introduction and called him 'the well-known apologist at Liberty University,' then said, 'I'm incurably incurious about overviews of trends,' before moving on. Habermas laughs it off.

boundaries.what_it_shows: Allison's ambivalence toward Habermas's overview work.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That Allison rejects Habermas's minimal facts or that the comment reflects scholarly consensus.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Allison did not write this or that the quote is misremembered.

narrative_arc.opening_device: Dale introduces the 'silly skeptical softball objection' about Habermas avoiding names on YouTube.
narrative_arc.central_tension: Habermas defends his scholarly method and citation practice against online skeptics who accuse him of bias, avoidance, and unscholarly behavior.
narrative_arc.resolution_or_payoff: Habermas demonstrates extensive citation, cites hostile witnesses, and explains his criteria, ending with a discussion of language limitations and the publication of his journal article.

stories.notes: The transcript is a conversational interview with two speakers (Dale and Gary Habermas). Stories are primarily illustrative and defensive, used to rebut criticisms and establish Habermas's scholarly credibility. No parables or thought experiments. Historical content is mostly anecdotal and not independently verified in the transcript.

core_relation.sentence: A belief in the resurrection is rationally justified only when a fact is highly evidenced AND a scholarly consensus supports it, with the evidential criterion being by far the more important of the two.
core_relation.quote: It's only when accompanied by high it being highly evidence that you can rationally believe. [S385]

product_test.quote: I think number one is so far ahead of number two that I think if number two disappears no biggie. [S403]
product_test.reason: Habermas explicitly states that criterion two (scholarly consensus) can disappear without significant loss, and that criterion one (high evidence) alone is 'sufficient for a rational belief' [S325]. This is additive weighting, not multiplicative collapse: the loss of one factor weakens but does not nullify the conclusion.

slots.plays_role: External negentropy influx: the outside source of coherence for the argument. In this paper, the external source is the body of published scholarly research (3,700 pages, 8,000 footnotes, multiple attestation, eyewitness and early creedal sources) that sustains the minimal facts against entropy (skeptical objections).
slots.quote: I've got feet and feet and feet of sources for this thing. 3,700 pages. [S185-S186]

slots.plays_role: Alignment: coupling is strongest when the system is aligned with its reference. Here, the 'reference' is the historical data, and scholars are valued when they align with the data regardless of their theological camp.
slots.quote: I try to go where the evidence leads and that's my I I hope a lot of us can say that's my credo. [S538]

slots.plays_role: Signal fidelity: whether truth survives transmission through noise. Habermas argues that the minimal facts survive transmission through hostile sources (Bultmann, the Jesus Seminar, atheist scholars) without distortion.
slots.quote: If you if you know where to look, these people aren't in the book because I generally don't go back to the to 1941 for sources, but you can find these guys and man admits himself way more than that. [S492]

slots.plays_role: Effective entropy: what lowers coherence. In this paper, entropy is the noise of bias, ad hominem attacks, and unfair skepticism that degrades the scholarly consensus.
slots.quote: It's the guys that are unfair that scream all the time and you go, 'Yeah, well that's what you fundamentalist do.' [S376]

slots.plays_role: Temporal integration: time turns possibility into accumulated consequence. Habermas emphasizes the early dating of creedal statements (within months of the crucifixion) and the long history of research from 1975 onward.
slots.quote: He says it was probably or may have been or likely have been he says it in different ways out within months. [S251]

slots.plays_role: Compression: ordered meaning compresses and noise does not. The minimal facts themselves are a compression of the vast evidence into six compact, highly attested propositions.
slots.quote: I can find my six facts over and over and over and over and over. [S439]

slots.plays_role: Phase transition: some thresholds change state, not just degree. Habermas describes a threshold of evidence beyond which belief becomes rational, though he refuses to name a percentage.
slots.quote: I do not have a certain threshold that they have to have to meet. [S206]

slots.plays_role: Superposition: open possibility stays unresolved until actualized. The paper treats the resurrection as a historical event that was once an open question but is now settled by evidence and consensus.
slots.quote: What about the resurrection? Is it not a myth? Pure and simple. [S504]

slots.plays_role: Non-local correlation: related systems are no longer independent. Habermas argues that scholars across ideological spectra (from Bultmann to evangelical) converge on the minimal facts, showing non-local correlation.
slots.quote: when guys who are not even in my camp, and he's not the only one will compliment something, um, I'm happy for it. [S371]

slots.plays_role: Integration: the local integrator inside the product. Habermas himself is the integrator, synthesizing 3,700 pages of research into a coherent argument.
slots.quote: I'm the author of these four volumes. I'm setting down my own criteria. [S659-S660]

master_equation.one_line: The paper's core relation is an additive two-criterion test for rational belief in the resurrection, where the evidential criterion dominates and the consensus criterion is optional, making the χ analogy weak because it lacks multiplicative collapse.
breaks: The product test is explicitly additive, not multiplicative: Habermas says if criterion two disappears 'no biggie' [S403], which contradicts the zero-collapse property of χ.
Slot R (phase transition) is stretched: Habermas refuses to define a threshold, saying 'I do not have a certain threshold' [S206], so there is no clear phase transition.
Slot Q (superposition) is stretched: the resurrection is treated as a settled historical fact, not an open possibility.

coherence.paper_uuid: Gary Habermas - Chapter 010 - What Scholars Believe About Jesus' Resurrection (Pt. 1) - Gary Habermas

overall.summary: The interview is largely internally consistent, with Habermas repeatedly clarifying that he does not use numerical thresholds for evidence or consensus, though minor tensions arise from his use of approximate percentages and the interviewer's framing.

dimensions.name: internal_consistency
reasons: Habermas consistently states he has never counted scholarly consensus percentages except for the empty tomb (S182, S300, S304, S307-S308), which aligns with A04.
He maintains that evidence (Criterion 1) is far more important than consensus (Criterion 2) (S326-S329), consistent with A02.
He asserts that consensus alone is not sufficient for rational belief (S385), matching A06.

However, he gives approximate percentages like '90 or 85% of the game' (S329) and mentions '90% or more' in the interviewer's question (S296), which creates minor tension with his claim of not using numbers.
He also says he is 'slanted toward liberal scholars' (S589) while claiming fairness (A10, A18), a mild tension but not a contradiction.

dimensions.name: definitional_stability
reasons: The definition of 'minimal fact' is clearly stated: strong evidence and majority scholarly agreement (A01, S166-S168).
Habermas defines 'critical scholar' by terminal degree and relevant field (S565-S567), and explains language criteria (S661, S664).
He clarifies that he does not use a numerical threshold for evidence (A03, S206, S214), though he uses categories like multiple attestation and eyewitnesses (S225-S228).
The term 'highly evidenced' is left somewhat vague, but he explains it through examples rather than a number (S207-S228).

dimensions.name: inferential_connectedness
reasons: The argument that consensus alone is insufficient is supported by the claim that consensus can be wrong (S407) and that evidence is primary (S326).
The connection between including non-evangelical scholars and avoiding bias is made explicit (A07, S049-S053, S589).
The rationale for language restriction is tied to authorial right and practical research languages (A05, S661, S664).
However, the inference from 'no numerical threshold' to 'I don't count' is not fully airtight, as he does give rough estimates (S329).

dimensions.name: register_boundary_respect
reasons: The conversation stays within the bounds of discussing scholarly method and the content of Habermas's volumes.
Habermas distinguishes between his books (where he cites names) and YouTube interviews (where he avoids names) (S027-S029), respecting different registers.
He acknowledges his own biases and editorial comments (A13, S096, S589), maintaining transparency.
No major category errors or inappropriate shifts in register are evident.

tensions.description: Habermas claims he does not use numerical thresholds or count consensus percentages, yet he gives approximate percentages (e.g., '90 or 85% of the game') and mentions '90% or more' in the interviewer's question. This is a tension between his stated method and his informal estimates.

Habermas claims his work is not biased and he tries to be fair, but he also admits he is 'slanted toward liberal scholars' (S589). This is a tension between impartiality and a deliberate slant, though he frames it as a corrective to avoid conservative bias.

missing_definitions.description: Habermas does not provide a precise definition or threshold for what counts as 'highly evidenced' (Criterion 1). He describes it through examples (multiple attestation, eyewitnesses, early sources) but no operational criteria.
The exact percentage or criteria for 'vast majority' in Criterion 2 is not specified, and Habermas explicitly avoids giving a number (S303-S304).

coherence.notes: The interview is a spoken conversation with auto-captions, so some repetition and informal language are expected. The coherence is generally high, with Habermas consistently clarifying his methodology. The main tensions are minor and stem from informal approximations versus strict methodological claims.
